title: Water and air in the pores
teaches: How pores of different sizes hold water or let it drain, why rain pools on some beds, and how long a bed lasts between waterings

blocks.text: The morning after a long soaking rain, one garden bed still has standing puddles while the bed beside it drank the rain straight in. A few sunny days later, that second bed has dried to dust. Both received the same downpour, so the difference comes down to the size of their pores—the empty spaces between the solid grains from lesson 1.

blocks.caption: The morning after a heavy rain: water still standing where the soil couldn't take it in

blocks.text: Pore size governs whether water drains away or stays put. Wide pores between coarse sand grains or soil crumbs hold water loosely, letting gravity pull it down and out within a day or two so fresh [[air|air]] can follow it in. Narrow pores tucked between silt and clay particles grip water so tightly against the mineral surfaces that gravity cannot pull it down,[^capillary] keeping those tiny spaces full long after the storm ends.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Wide pores let excess water drain and fill with [[air|air]], while narrow pores hold onto [[water|water]].

blocks.text: A day or two after a heavy soaking, once gravity has drained the wide pores, the soil holds as much [[water|water]] as it can keep on its own—a stage soil scientists call **field capacity**.[^field-capacity] Plant roots draw from that stored supply, though they can never drink the soil bone-dry. The final fraction of moisture clings to microscopic pores and clay surfaces with more force than any root can overcome, so a crop will wilt even when the soil still feels cool and slightly damp. That lower limit is the **wilting point**, and the moisture sitting between field capacity and the wilting point is the share a plant can actually use.

blocks.caption: The pore space in the top 30 cm of three beds once a soaking has drained
blocks.task: Raise the organic matter to 5% and watch the sandy and clay beds

blocks.text: Notice how the three textures behave in the chart. [[Sand|sand]] drains right away and stores very little moisture. [[Clay|clay]] holds a huge total volume of water, yet it locks a large fraction away in microscopic pores and drains so slowly that roots can suffocate while waiting for air to return. Loams strike a balance, pairing enough small pores to store moisture with enough wide ones to drain promptly.[^silt-water] While you cannot swap out a bed's mineral texture, building up its [[organic matter|organic]] shores up whichever weakness a soil has: sandy beds hold more usable water, and heavy clay beds drain several times faster.[^model]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Plants can only draw the water held between field capacity and the wilting point, leaving the tightest pore water behind.

blocks.text: Whenever rain falls faster than the soil surface can soak it up, the excess water pools in low spots or runs off downslope, washing away the finest, most fertile particles at the top. How quickly a bed drinks in a storm depends on having wide, connected pores leading down from the surface: coarse sand can swallow a summer cloudburst, whereas dense clay can puddle during a steady drizzle.

blocks.caption: An hour of rain on a bed
blocks.task: Find a rain that makes a puddle

blocks.text: On a real garden bed, the condition of the very top millimetre often matters more than the soil underneath. Heavy raindrops slamming into bare dirt shatter surface crumbs into loose silt and clay, which wash into the surface pores and dry into a tight crust that sheds the next storm.[^raindrop] Keeping the bed covered with mulch or leafy crops breaks the fall of the rain so the surface stays open, while earthworm burrows and decayed root channels act as vertical drainpipes (a job covered in lesson 3).

The same limit applies when watering by hand or with a sprinkler. Flooding a bed faster than its pores can drink simply sends water running down the garden path, so slow-draining clay or crusted beds take water best through a drip line, a soaker hose, or a watering can poured in stages with a pause to let each pass soak in.

On a warm, breezy summer day, a full bed of vegetables goes through roughly 5 mm of water—equivalent to 5 litres, or half a large watering can, spread over every square metre. Nearly all of that water is pulled up by the roots and transpired out through the leaves to cool the plant, leaving the soil pores as the crop's only water tank between rains.

blocks.caption: Three beds soaked once and left in the summer sun: the usable water remaining day by day

blocks.text: Because different textures store very different reserves, watering works best when you soak the bed thoroughly and wait several days before watering again. Pouring on 20 to 25 litres per square metre (two full watering cans) wets a loam 15 to 20 cm deep, reaching deeper in sand and slightly shallower in clay; you can push a trowel into the bed an hour later to check how far the damp front travelled. Sprinkling a little water every evening only dampens the top few centimetres, encouraging shallow roots that bake as soon as the sun comes out, whereas soaking the bed once or twice a week draws roots down into deeper, cooler reserves.[^roots-deep] On fast-draining sandy beds, pairing deep watering with surface mulch and compost slows evaporation and adds moisture-holding pores.

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: To test your drainage rate with a tin can, cut both ends off a can, push it 5 cm into the soil, and fill it with 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water. If it drains in under 10 minutes, the bed is fast-draining and likely sandy; if it takes longer than an hour, the pores are tight or compacted (lessons 5 and 8 cover how to fix this).

To check whether a bed needs watering, dig down a trowel's depth and squeeze a handful of soil. Soil that crumbles dry needs a soak, soil that holds a loose ball and leaves your palm cool and damp has plenty of moisture, and soil that drips water is too wet to dig or walk on.

blocks.caption: Eight questions on water and air in soil

items.question: What fills the wide pores of a soil a couple of days after a soaking?
items.why: Gravity pulls water out of the wide pores within a day or two, drawing fresh air down behind it while the narrow pores stay filled with water.

items.question: A plant is wilting, but the soil around its roots still feels slightly damp. Why?
options: The remaining water is held too tightly for the roots to pull out
The plant is getting too much air
Damp soil has no water in it
items.why: The last films of water cling to microscopic pores and clay surfaces with more suction than crop roots can overcome, meaning the bed has reached its wilting point.

items.question: Water pools on this bed whenever it rains hard. What is happening?
options: Rain is falling faster than the surface pores can carry it down
There is too much air in the soil
items.why: Puddles form when rain outpaces infiltration—usually because the bed is heavy clay, sealed by a surface crust, or packed down underneath.

items.question: Which of these soils holds the most water that a plant can actually use?
items.why: Loams combine plenty of medium and small pores to store usable moisture with enough wide pores to let excess water drain. Sand and gravel let water run straight through.

items.question: What does a heavy rainstorm do to bare soil?
options: Shatters surface crumbs and washes fine grains into the pores, sealing them
items.why: Falling raindrops hit bare dirt hard enough to break soil crumbs apart, and the loose silt and clay plug the surface pores into a crust. Mulch or plant leaves absorb the impact.

items.question: Why is it better to water deeply once or twice a week than lightly every evening?
options: Deep watering encourages roots to grow down into a larger moisture reserve
Daily watering washes all the clay out of the bed
Vegetables only take up water once a week
items.why: Light daily sprinkles only wet the top few centimetres—the layer that dries out fastest in the sun—while deep soakings draw roots down where moisture lasts.

items.question: Roughly how much water does it take to give one square metre of bed a thorough soaking?
options: About 20 to 25 litres (two full watering cans)
items.why: Pouring 20 to 25 litres onto a square metre equals 20 to 25 mm of rainfall, enough to wet a loamy bed 15 to 20 cm deep right through the main root zone.

items.question: In the tin can test, 2.5 cm of water takes three hours to soak away. What does that tell you?
options: The soil has very few wide pores—likely from heavy clay, a surface crust, or compaction
The bed is an open, crumbly loam
items.why: Slow infiltration means the wide drainage pores are missing or blocked. Lessons 5 and 8 cover how to diagnose and open up slow beds.

summary: **Pore size decides water or air.** Wide pores drain by gravity and fill with air; narrow pores hold water against it.
**Plants can use only part of the water.** The reserve lies between field capacity and the wilting point; the tightest-held water stays behind.
**Loams hold the most usable water.** More than sands, which drain it away, or heavy clays, which hold it too tightly.
**Water faster than the soil takes it and it runs off.** Rain or irrigation that outpaces the wide pores pools on the surface.
**Water deeply and less often.** Soak beds once or twice a week, keep the surface covered, and check with a trowel before watering.
**Simple tests tell you what you have.** A tin-can infiltration test shows drainage; a squeezed handful shows moisture.

capillary.title: Capillarity
capillary.text: Water molecules are attracted both to mineral surfaces (adhesion) and to one another (cohesion). Inside a narrow pore, that combined pull overcomes gravity, just as water climbs up a narrow glass tube or wicks into a paper towel. The narrower the pore, the tighter the grip—a force soil scientists measure as **matric potential** (or soil suction).

field-capacity.title: Field capacity and wilting point
field-capacity.text: In lab measurements, **field capacity** is defined as the water remaining in a soil against a suction of 10 to 33 kilopascals (up to a third of an atmosphere, with 10 kPa often used for coarse sands and 33 kPa for finer soils). The **permanent wilting point** is the water still clinging at 1,500 kilopascals (15 atmospheres)—the maximum suction most vegetable crops can exert before they fail to recover overnight. The water held between those two pressures is **plant-available water**.

silt-water.title: Why silt holds the most usable water
silt-water.text: While clay holds the highest *total* amount of water, so much of it is locked inside microscopic pores below the wilting point that plants cannot reach it. Medium-sized pores between silt grains and fine crumbs hold water tightly enough to resist gravity (above field capacity) yet loosely enough for roots to drink easily, giving loams and silt loams the largest supply of plant-available water.

model.title: Where the figure's numbers come from
model.text: The interactive chart uses the pedotransfer equations published by Keith Saxton and Walter Rawls (2006), calibrated across thousands of US soil samples to estimate field capacity, wilting point, total porosity, and saturated drainage rate from sand, clay, and organic matter percentages. Real garden beds can drain even faster than the equations predict when earthworms and roots open up continuous channels.

raindrop.title: The force of a raindrop
raindrop.text: A large raindrop hits the ground at around 9 metres per second (over 30 km/h), roughly the top speed of a sprinter. On bare dirt, each drop acts like a tiny bomb that blasts soil grains up to half a metre through the air. Over a single heavy storm, raindrop splash can dislodge tonnes of topsoil per hectare, clogging surface pores and starting sheet erosion.

roots-deep.title: How deep roots go
roots-deep.text: Given loose, aerated soil, vegetable roots reach much deeper than a spade's blade. Lettuce and onions stay mostly in the top 30 cm, but tomatoes, squash, and carrots can send roots a metre down, and winter wheat or lucerne (alfalfa) can reach past two metres. Even though the densest root mat feeds in the top 30 cm, those deeper explorer roots keep the plant alive during a summer heatwave.
